subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Obtain the reduction formula for I_n = ∫ cosecⁿx dx, and hence find ∫ cosec⁵x dx.

mark_split.label: Apply by parts and use cot²x = csc²x − 1
Substitute n = 5, 3, 1 for the final answer

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B, book printed p.28 (PDF page 27) — LAQ chapter 3 ‘Integration’, answer 18.2, the twin of 18.1 on the same ★★★ SSP 28 page. Printed appearances: AP 19 · TS 19 (partly obscured by a sticker in the scan; TS year read from the visible fragment). Chapter star rank ★★★. no printed margin mark tags or tick-box splits appear anywhere in the Integration LAQ chapter (book pp.26-37) — this card's mark split is OURS, patterned on the 7-mark shapes printed elsewhere in the book (e.g. 2+2+2+1, 1+1+2+2+1). Where this book is wrong — the task's own flagged suspect, confirmed: the book's printed final line drops the leading minus sign on the −csc³x·cotx/4 term, printing it as though the term were positive, even though the SAME derivation's immediately preceding lines (‘I₅ = −csc³x cotx/4 + …’) carry that minus sign correctly. Differentiating the book's printed (unsigned) final line does not return csc⁵x; differentiating −csc³x cotx/4 − (3/8)cscx cotx + (3/8)log|tan(x/2)| + c does. This card keeps the mathematically correct minus sign and records the book's printed slip here. No two-book union check and no board back-test were possible for Maths-2B (no second-year TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand; the book's five Guess Papers pp.118-127 stand in for the back-test).

insider_note: This is the one reduction in the chapter where the book's own printed final answer needs a correction — double check the sign on the csc³x·cotx term against this card's boxed line before copying it into an exam script.

steps.label: Set up integration by parts
steps.why: Peeling off csc²x (whose antiderivative is the known −cotx) leaves cscⁿ⁻²x to differentiate — the cosecant partner of the secⁿx split, now carrying a minus sign because ∫csc²x dx = −cotx.
common_mistakes: Writing ∫cosec²x dx = +cotx, dropping the minus sign that belongs to this integral (unlike sec²x, which integrates to plain tanx).
Peeling off only one cscx instead of csc²x.
steps.memory_tip: ∫cosec²x dx = −cotx (minus); ∫sec²x dx = +tanx (plus) — the two twins differ here.

steps.label: Apply by parts and use cot²x = csc²x − 1
steps.why: cot²x = csc²x − 1 closes the loop back to I_n and I_{n−2} exactly as tan²x = sec²x − 1 does for secⁿx, but every term here carries the extra minus sign picked up in the setup step.
common_mistakes: Dropping the minus sign carried from step 1 partway through this expansion.
Writing cot²x = 1 − csc²x with the sign reversed.
steps.memory_tip: Copy secⁿx's working, then put a minus sign in front of every single term — that is the whole difference.

steps.label: Solve for the reduction formula
steps.why: Same algebra as secⁿx — collect I_n terms, divide by (n−1) — but the first term keeps the minus sign that was present from the very first line of this derivation.
common_mistakes: Losing the minus sign in front of cosecⁿ⁻²x cotx/(n−1) at this step — this is exactly where the book's own printed error happens two steps later.
steps.memory_tip: The minus sign on the first term must survive every line to the very end — that is this question's whole trap.

steps.label: Substitute n = 5, 3, 1 for the final answer
steps.why: Odd n stops at I₁ = ∫cosecx dx = log|tan(x/2)|, the cosecant's own standard result — and the leading minus sign from every earlier line must still be there on the boxed final answer.
common_mistakes: Dropping the leading minus sign on −cosec³x cotx/4 in the final line — this is precisely the book's own printed slip; a differentiation check catches it immediately.
Writing log|tan(x/2)| as log|tanx/2| without the half-angle grouping, which is a different function.
steps.memory_tip: Differentiate the final answer to check: only −cosec³x cotx/4 − (3/8)cosecx cotx + (3/8)log|tan(x/2)| gives back cosec⁵x.
